summary: Proposes a simple, easily implemented protocol for making work across several cooperating nodes happen atomically, so every node reaches the same conclusion on whether to complete or abandon it, even with failures.

eli5.summary: A way for several people to all agree to do something together or all agree to cancel, so no one is left half done.

subtitle: A small two-phase commit protocol that lets transaction managers on different Internet nodes agree to complete or abandon shared work.

tldr.problem: Different nodes that cooperate on work need every node to reach the same conclusion on whether to complete it, even with failures. Earlier two-phase commit protocols were too complex and bundled with specific communication stacks, so none became widely used on the Internet.
tldr.mechanism: TIP runs over TCP, optionally with TLS, as simple one-line ASCII commands between transaction managers. It specifies only how nodes agree on the outcome, while the work itself travels over other protocols.
tldr.outcome: Heterogeneous transaction managers can implement TIP to talk to each other, and applications can share a transaction by passing a tip:// URL. The RFC does not expect it to replace existing protocols.

today: RFC 2371 is a Proposed Standard published in July 1998, and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. Supplemental requirements and background are in RFC 2372.

sections.title: Why a Simple Two-Phase Commit
sections.content:
The standard way to get atomic commitment is the two-phase commit protocol. Many implementations exist, but none became widely used on the Internet, mainly because of complexity: the commit protocol was bundled with a specific program-to-program communication protocol that lived on a large infrastructure.

TIP gets its simplicity by specifying only how nodes agree on the outcome of a transaction. The subject matter they agree on is communicated by other protocols, which avoids application communication semantics and data representation. It is envisioned mainly for one node's transaction manager to talk to another's. The RFC does not expect TIP to replace existing protocols, but expects many heterogeneous transaction managers to be able to implement it.

The RFC's example is an online store. A server placing several orders starts a transaction with its local transaction manager and passes a reference to it, as user data on HTTP requests, to the other servers involved. They ask their transaction managers to join. If the transaction commits, all orders were placed; if it aborts, none were.
sections.eli5: Many old systems that make a group all say yes or all say no were so complicated that hardly anyone used them. TIP keeps just the yes-or-no part and leaves everything else to other tools.

sections.title: Transactions, Push and Pull
sections.content:
A transaction is a programming model where work has atomic semantics: either all of it completes and its changes become permanent (the transaction commits), or, if any work fails, the changes are undone (it aborts). The application defines the unit of work.

There is no single globally accepted format for transaction identifiers. Each party in a superior/subordinate relationship assigns its own identifier, and they are exchanged when the relationship is first established, so a manager can use its own format internally.

A program on node A can bring node B into a transaction in two ways. In the push model, A's transaction manager asks B's manager to instantiate the transaction as a subordinate and return its name for it. In the pull model, A just tells B to do work as part of the transaction A's manager knows by some name, and B's manager then enlists by pulling the transaction from A. Either way A's manager learns to involve B's in the two-phase commit. TIP supports both.
sections.eli5: Either everyone finishes the group project or everybody throws away their part. To join, you can either be invited by the leader (push) or knock on the leader's door and ask to join (pull).

sections.title: Addresses, URLs and Connections
sections.content:
TIP needs a reliable ordered stream transport with low connection setup cost. On the Internet it runs over TCP, optionally with TLS for security and optionally with a multiplexing protocol to carry light-weight connections over one TCP or TLS connection. A different connection is used for each simultaneous transaction between two managers, and a connection can be reused once its transaction ends.

A transaction manager address has the form <hostport><path>. The host is a DNS name or IP address, with an optional port; if omitted, the standard TIP port 3372 is used. The path identifies the specific manager at that location. How a manager first learns an address is left to the implementation.

After connecting, the primary issues IDENTIFY with its own address and the secondary's address. The primary address lets the secondary reconnect after a failure; without it, the primary must not do anything needing a reconnection.

Applications share transactions using a TIP URL: tip://<transaction manager address>?<transaction string>. The string is either a standard URN form (urn:<NID>:<NSS>, per RFC 2141) or a printable ASCII identifier, in which case the address and identifier together make it globally unique. TIP URLs must be unique for all time, for example by including a UUID. The TIP protocol itself does not use the URL scheme; it is for passing transaction information through other protocols.
sections.eli5: Each transaction manager has an address like a phone number, and a TIP link is like a note saying whom to call and which group project you mean. The note must never be confused with any other note.

sections.title: Connection States and Roles
sections.content:
At any instant only the primary on a connection may send commands; the secondary only responds. The side that opened the connection starts as primary, and a few commands swap the roles. The roles return to their original polarity whenever the Idle state is reached. Normally only the primary closes a connection, in the Initial state.

A connection is always in one of these states: Initial (only IDENTIFY or TLS allowed), Idle (no transaction; BEGIN, MULTIPLEX, PUSH, PULL, QUERY, RECONNECT allowed), Begun (one-phase completion only), Enlisted (one-phase or two-phase), Prepared, Multiplexing, Tls and Error. Failure of a connection in Begun or Enlisted state implies the transaction will be aborted. Unlike the others, failure in Prepared state does not automatically abort. Multiplexing, Tls and Error can never be left.

The protocol is versioned: the primary sends the lowest and highest versions it understands in IDENTIFY, the secondary replies with its highest, and the smaller of the two highest is used. This document describes version 3.
sections.eli5: On each phone line only one person is allowed to ask questions at a time, while the other answers. The line also remembers which step of the plan you are on, and some steps cannot be undone by a dropped call.

sections.title: Commands and Responses
sections.content:
Every command and response is one line of ASCII (octets 32 through 126) ending in a CR or LF. The first word, in upper case, is the type; each takes a fixed number of parameters, and anything after the first undefined word is ignored and may carry human-readable debug text. Lines may be pipelined and sent together; receivers must support this, and a line that arrives out of turn is held until the connection state needs it. A line that causes an error puts the connection in the Error state.

Connection commands are IDENTIFY, MULTIPLEX and TLS. Transaction commands are ABORT, BEGIN, COMMIT, PREPARE, PULL, PUSH, QUERY and RECONNECT.

  • PUSH or PULL establishes a superior/subordinate relationship (answered by PUSHED, ALREADYPUSHED or PULLED); the connection enters Enlisted.
  • PREPARE is phase one. The subordinate answers PREPARED, ABORTED (it vetoes) or READONLY (it no longer cares).
  • COMMIT in the Prepared state tells the subordinate the transaction committed. In Begun or Enlisted it is a one-phase request, and should only be used when the sender has no local recoverable resources and only one subordinate.
  • BEGIN asks the secondary to create a new transaction completed in one phase.
sections.eli5: The messages are short lines of plain text such as PREPARE, then PREPARED, then COMMIT. First everyone says they are ready, then the leader says go.

sections.title: Failure and Recovery
sections.content:
Any party that cannot understand a line closes the connection, and an ERROR command or response puts the connection in the Error state. A closed connection is treated as a communication failure; how to detect one is private to the implementation.

Failures in Initial or Idle state need no action. If a connection fails in Begun or Enlisted state and COMMIT was not sent, the transaction aborts. If COMMIT was sent, the subordinate holds the outcome, and the superior uses application-specific means to find it.

The hard case is failure in Prepared state. If the superior decides to commit, it must eventually open a new connection and send RECONNECT; on NOTRECONNECTED it is done, on RECONNECTED it must send COMMIT and receive COMMITTED. If it decides to abort, it may reconnect and should send ABORT. A subordinate that notices the failure should periodically connect to the superior and send QUERY until it gets QUERIEDNOTFOUND (then it should abort) or the superior sends RECONNECT.
sections.eli5: If the phone line drops after everyone said "ready", the leader calls back later to tell them the result. Anyone left waiting keeps calling to ask whether the plan still exists.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Security applied to the application protocol can be subverted unless matching security applies to the commitment protocol. TLS gives optional client and server authentication and optional encryption. An implementation may refuse service unless TLS is used, encryption is on, or the remote party is authenticated, and it should be willing to be authenticated itself.

The RFC lists specific attacks and mitigations:

  • PULL denial of service: someone who knows an active transaction's identity can PULL it and drop the connection, causing an abort. Refuse PULL unless TLS, authentication and trust are in place.
  • PUSH denial of service: repeatedly creating transactions, reaching Prepared and dropping the connection can exhaust resources. The same mitigation applies to PUSH.
  • Transaction corruption: an attacker could send RECONNECT then COMMIT or ABORT. Record the superior's authenticated identity and accept RECONNECT only from it, over TLS.
  • Sniffing and man-in-the-middle: use TLS for encryption and authentication, and put no personalizing information on the TLS/TLSING exchange.
sections.eli5: A stranger could pretend to be part of the group and ruin the plan, or listen in. The advice is to check who you are talking to and keep the conversation private.

sections.title: TIP Multiplexing Protocol
sections.content:
Appendix A defines the TIP Multiplexing Protocol (TMP) version 2.0, which is optional to implement and the only multiplexing protocol TIP 3.0 supports. The primary offers it with MULTIPLEX TMP2.0. The secondary answers MULTIPLEXING or CANTMULTIPLEX. It exists because short-lived transactions make TCP setup and teardown costly, including delays from TCP's congestion control.

A TMP packet has a 64 bit header with a flag byte, a connection identifier and a packet length, followed by data. Connection identifiers are 24 bit integers; the side that opened the TCP connection uses even ones, the other side odd. A TIP command must fit wholly within one TMP packet. The RFC says TMP is not a generalized multiplexing protocol: large messages could overflow buffering and deadlock, which TIP avoids because it is request-response with short messages.
sections.eli5: Instead of opening a new phone line for every short chat, TMP lets many short chats share one line by labelling each message with the chat it belongs to.
